message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact speed right now.  
But you can check it yourself in a few quick ways:

---

## 1️⃣ Quick Online Speed Test  
The easiest method is to use a web‑based speed‑testing service.

| Site | How to Use |
|------|------------|
| **Speedtest by Ookla** – <https://www.speedtest.net> | Open the page, click “Go” and wait for the test to finish. |
| **Fast.com** – <https://fast.com> | The test starts automatically; you’ll see download speed, then click “Show more” for upload and ping. |
| **Google Speed Test** – type “speed test” into Google and click the “Run Speed Test” button that appears. |

These sites measure:
- **Download speed** (how fast data comes in)
- **Upload speed** (how fast data goes out)
- **Ping / latency** (how quickly a request is acknowledged)

---

## 2️⃣ Command‑Line Test (Windows)  

If you prefer a terminal approach, you can use PowerShell or `curl`/`wget`.  
Below is a simple PowerShell script that downloads a file from a public server and reports the speed.

```powershell
# PowerShell (run as Administrator or normal user)
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$dest = "$env:TEMP\test.bin"

$sw = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile $dest
$sw.Stop()

$bytes = (Get-Item $dest).Length
$seconds = $sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes / 1MB) / $seconds

Write-Host "Downloaded $([math]::Round($bytes / 1MB, 2)) MB in $([math]::Round($seconds, 2)) s"
Write-Host "≈ $([math]::Round($mbps, 2)) MB/s"
```

**What it does**

1. Downloads a 100 MB file from Hetzner’s public speed‑test server.  
2. Measures the time taken.  
3. Calculates megabytes per second (MB/s).  
4. Prints the result.

> **Tip:** If you want a more accurate test, run it a few times and average the results.

---

## 3️⃣ Using `speedtest-cli` (Python)

If you have Python installed, you can install the official CLI tool:

```bash
pip install speedtest-cli
```

Then run:

```bash
speedtest
```

It will automatically pick the nearest server, test download/upload speeds, and show ping.

---

## 4️⃣ Router/Modem Interface

Many consumer routers expose a status page that shows current link speed:

1. Open a browser and go to your router’s IP (commonly `192.168.1.1`, `192.168.0.1`, or `10.0.0.1`).  
2. Log in (default credentials are often on the back of the device).  
3. Look for a “Status”, “Internet”, or “WAN” section.  
4. It usually lists “Link Speed” (e.g., 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps).

> **Note:** This shows the *physical* link speed, not the actual throughput you experience.

---

## 5️⃣ Mobile Apps

If you’re on a phone, there are many free apps that perform speed tests:

- **Speedtest by Ookla** (Android & iOS)
- **Fast.com** (Android & iOS)
- **OpenSignal** (Android & iOS)

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | What You Get | How Easy |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| Web site (Speedtest, Fast.com) | Full download/upload + ping | Very easy |
| PowerShell script | Download speed (MB/s) | Medium |
| `speedtest-cli` | Full test via CLI | Medium |
| Router status page | Physical link speed | Easy |
| Mobile app | Full test on the go | Very easy |

Pick the one that fits your setup. If you run into any trouble or need help interpreting the results, just let me know!
